{"problem": {"theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "candidate_text": "Take \(c=\frac27\) and \(d=5\).

For the lower bound, assume \(n\ge3\). There are \(n(n-2)\) horizontal and \(n(n-2)\) vertical triples, hence \(2n(n-2)\) potential blocks. In a terminal configuration every such triple contains a removed stamp.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal triples: their starting columns range from two columns before the block to two columns after its start. Each of its three stamps belongs to at most three vertical triples, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most \(14\) potential triples. The same bound holds for a vertical block. Consequently, if \(m\) blocks have been removed,
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
This applies in particular to \(b(n)\). For \(n=1,2\), we have \(b(n)=0\), and the same inequality still holds.

For the upper bound, first consider the infinite integer grid. In row \(r\), designate the disjoint horizontal blocks
\[
(r,r+5k),\ (r,r+5k+1),\ (r,r+5k+2),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Thus a cell \((r,j)\) is designated precisely when
\[
j-r\pmod 5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
The undesignated residues are \(3,4\). Hence no three consecutive cells in a row are all undesignated. In a fixed column, as \(r\) increases, \(j-r\pmod5\) runs through consecutive residues in reverse order, so again no three consecutive cells are all undesignated. Therefore every horizontal or vertical triple in the infinite grid meets a designated cell.

Now retain only those designated horizontal blocks lying completely inside the \(n\times n\) sheet, and tear them out. In each row there are at most
\[
\left\lceil\frac{n-2}{5}\right\rceil\le \frac n5+1
\]
such blocks, so initially fewer than or equal to \(n^2/5+n\) blocks are removed.

A designated cell inside the sheet whose designated block was not retained must lie in one of the first two or last two columns. Consequently, every triple surviving the initial removals meets the set \(S\) consisting of those boundary columns, where \(|S|\le4n\). Continue greedily removing any surviving triple until none remains. Every additionally removed triple was already present after the initial removals and therefore contains a cell of \(S\). Since the added blocks are disjoint, there can be at most \(|S|\le4n\) of them.

Thus a terminal configuration is obtained using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Hence
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le\frac15n^2+5n
\]
for every positive integer \(n\), proving the theorem."}
